enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Subject-specific autonomic baseline variability leads to different signal-to-noise ratios in wearable stress signals.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Individual differences in resting heart rate variability and skin conductance level alter the dynamic range of stress-induced changes, making the same absolute change represent different signal-to-noise ratios across subjects.
rival_explanations: Differences in stressor intensity across subjects rather than baseline physiology
Sensor hardware variability between devices
Preprocessing pipeline differences (e.g., filtering settings)
minimum_data_needed: Per-subject baseline autonomic measures (HRV, SCL) collected under standardized conditions
Repeated labeled stress episodes per subject
Within-subject repeated measures to separate within- vs between-subject variance
Concurrent medication and substance use logs
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Baseline autonomic tone (indexed by resting HRV and SCL) modulates the dynamic range of stress-induced physiological changes. After controlling for age, fitness, medication, caffeine, and time of day, the residual between-subject variance in baseline autonomic tone predicts the signal-to-noise ratio of wearable stress features. The stress detection model should include individual baseline HRV and SCL as normalization covariates, and prediction intervals should be scaled by subject-specific baseline variability.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Baseline measures must be taken under controlled conditions (supine, quiet, fasting). Medication and substance use are critical confounders because they directly alter autonomic tone. Fitness level affects resting HRV independently of stress reactivity.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Variability in sensor placement tightness and skin contact introduces subject-specific motion artifact profiles.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Looser wristbands allow greater relative motion between sensor and skin, amplifying motion artifacts that mimic or mask stress-related physiological changes.
possible_confounders: Activity type (typing vs. running vs. weightlifting)
Device model and strap material (silicone, leather, metal)
control_variables: Self-reported tightness rating (1-5 scale) per wear session
Accelerometer-derived motion magnitude (RMS) during stress windows
Strap type and device model identifier
rival_explanations: Motion artifacts driven primarily by activity intensity, not tightness
Sensor hardware differences (e.g., LED wavelength, photodiode sensitivity)
Software filtering differences across firmware versions
minimum_data_needed: Daily tightness self-reports or objective proxy (e.g., strap tension sensor)
Synchronized triaxial accelerometer data at same sampling rate as PPG/EDA
Wrist circumference and strap type per subject
Per-subject motion artifact labels (e.g., from video or manual annotation)
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Strap tightness modulates the coupling between skin motion and sensor motion. Looser fit increases the transfer function from wrist acceleration to PPG/EDA artifact amplitude. After controlling for activity intensity (accelerometer RMS), wrist circumference, and strap type, the residual tightness effect predicts subject-specific artifact contamination. The detection model should include tightness as a time-varying covariate and use accelerometer data to regress out motion artifacts via adaptive filtering.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Tightness is likely time-varying within subject (e.g., loosens during day). Objective tightness measures (e.g., strap force sensor) would strengthen inference. Strap material affects elasticity and should be standardized or recorded.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Individual differences in sweat gland density and distribution affect skin conductance signal quality and stress detectability.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Higher eccrine gland density yields larger, faster conductance responses to sympathetic activation, improving classifier confidence; lower density yields noisier, attenuated signals.
possible_confounders: Body site (wrist vs. finger vs. palm)
control_variables: Baseline skin conductance level (SCL) at rest
rival_explanations: Differences in central sympathetic reactivity unrelated to peripheral gland density
Electrode-skin contact impedance variation due to skin oil or dead skin
Signal processing artifacts (e.g., improper downsampling)
minimum_data_needed: Quantitative sudomotor function test (e.g., QSART, pilocarpine iontophoresis) or validated proxy
Baseline SCL and stress-evoked SCR amplitude per subject
Environmental logs (temperature, humidity) synchronized with recordings
Repeated stress trials to estimate within-subject SCR reliability
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Eccrine gland density determines the transduction gain from sympathetic sudomotor nerve activity to measurable skin conductance. After controlling for skin hydration, ambient conditions, age, and measurement site, the residual between-subject variance in gland density (proxied by maximal SCR amplitude to standardized stimulus) predicts the signal-to-noise ratio of stress-evoked EDA features. The classifier should normalize SCR amplitude by individual maximum response capacity and include baseline SCL as a covariate.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Direct gland density measurement is invasive; maximal SCR to a standardized stimulus (e.g., deep breath, startle) is a practical proxy. Hydration and environment strongly affect baseline SCL and must be logged. Site standardization is critical because wrist gland density is lower than palm.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Circadian phase shifts cause time-of-day dependent model performance that differs across subjects.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Autonomic regulation follows circadian rhythms; subjects with shifted chronotypes experience stress at different circadian phases, altering baseline physiology and classifier calibration.
possible_confounders: Sleep schedule variability (shift work, social jetlag)
Light exposure history (bright light at night)
control_variables: Actigraphy-derived sleep midpoint and duration for 7+ days
Time since awakening at each stress label
rival_explanations: Time-of-day effects driven by diurnal activity patterns rather than circadian phase
Stressor occurrence frequency varies by time of day (e.g., work hours)
Model training data biased toward certain times of day
minimum_data_needed: Chronotype assessment per subject
Actigraphy or sleep diary for at least one week
Timestamped stress labels with concurrent physiological data
Model performance metrics stratified by time-of-day and chronotype group
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Circadian phase (estimated from sleep midpoint, light exposure, and time since awakening) modulates baseline autonomic tone and stress reactivity. Subjects with later chronotypes experience a phase delay such that a given clock time corresponds to an earlier circadian phase, altering HRV and EDA baselines. After controlling for sleep timing, light exposure, and time since awakening, the mismatch between model training distribution (often daytime) and subject-specific circadian phase predicts degraded performance. The model should include circadian phase as a feature (e.g., hours since dim-light melatonin onset proxy) or stratify by chronotype.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Chronotype questionnaires have limitations; actigraphy-derived sleep midpoint is a better behavioral proxy. Dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) is gold standard but impractical; use validated proxy (e.g., sleep midpoint on free days). Model retraining per circadian phase bin may be needed.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Self-reported stress labels contain subject-specific recall bias, creating heterogeneous label noise.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Individuals differ in meta-cognitive awareness and reporting style; some under-report, others over-report stress, leading to systematic label errors that degrade model certainty differently per subject.
possible_confounders: Cognitive load at time of reporting
Survey timing relative to stressor (immediate vs. end-of-day recall)
control_variables: Validated personality questionnaires (Big Five, TAS-20 for alexithymia)
Momentary mood ratings (PANAS) at each EMA prompt
EMA compliance rate (prompts answered / prompts delivered)
rival_explanations: Label noise due to ambiguous stress definition in study instructions
Technical issues: missed prompts, notification fatigue
Random forgetting rather than systematic bias
minimum_data_needed: Personality and alexithymia assessments per subject
Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) with varying delays (immediate, 1h, end-of-day)
Physiological ground truth for a subset (e.g., lab stressor with known timing)
EMA metadata: response time, compliance, device timestamps
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Subject-specific reporting bias arises from stable traits (alexithymia, neuroticism) and state factors (mood, cognitive load). After controlling for these, the residual bias correlates with label noise variance. High alexithymia leads to under-reporting (false negatives); high neuroticism leads to over-reporting (false positives). The model should incorporate a measurement error model where label noise parameters are predicted by personality traits, and use multiple label sources (physiological arousal + self-report) to calibrate.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Alexithymia (TAS-20) is a strong predictor of interoceptive awareness deficits. EMA compliance must be high (>80%) to avoid selection bias. Lab calibration with known stressors (e.g., TSST) provides ground truth for bias estimation.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Unobserved subpopulations (e.g., anxiety disorders, medication use) create heterogeneous stress response patterns.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Clinical conditions or pharmacologic agents alter autonomic reactivity, producing distinct physiological signatures that the generic model cannot capture, inflating uncertainty for affected subjects.
possible_confounders: Socioeconomic status affecting healthcare access and diagnosis
rival_explanations: Heterogeneity due to random physiological variation
Model underfitting (insufficient capacity to capture complex patterns)
Sensor or data quality issues correlated with subpopulation
minimum_data_needed: Clinical screening data for all subjects
Medication records (prescription and OTC)
Diagnosed condition history
Sufficient per-subject physiological data to fit subject-specific response profiles
Ideally: clinical diagnosis confirmation for a subset
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Unobserved clinical subpopulations (e.g., generalized anxiety disorder, beta-blocker users) have distinct autonomic response signatures (blunted or exaggerated HRV/EDA reactivity). After screening for and controlling known conditions and medications, residual heterogeneity can be modeled via finite mixture models or hierarchical clustering on physiological response features. The detection model should include clinical covariates as fixed effects and allow subject-specific random effects on stress reactivity parameters.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Screening questionnaires (GAD-7, PHQ-9) are not diagnostic but identify probable cases. Medication class (beta-blockers, SSRIs, stimulants) has known autonomic effects. Substance use (nicotine) acutely affects HRV. Socioeconomic status may proxy for undiagnosed conditions.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Statistical model misspecification: assuming homoscedastic errors when residual variance is subject-dependent.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: A single global variance parameter underestimates uncertainty for high-variance subjects and overestimates for low-variance subjects, leading to miscalibrated prediction intervals.
possible_confounders: Non-stationary variance (variance changes over study duration)
Outliers from motion artifacts or device errors
control_variables: Subject-specific residual variance estimates (from preliminary model)
Activity level (accelerometer) during each prediction window
rival_explanations: Misspecification due to omitted variable bias (not heteroscedasticity per se)
Non-linear relationships modeled as linear
Autocorrelation inflating apparent heteroscedasticity
minimum_data_needed: Sufficient per-subject observations (>=30 stress windows) to estimate individual variance
Repeated measures across varying conditions (activity, time of day, stress levels)
Model residuals from a well-specified mean model
Diagnostics: residual vs. fitted plots per subject, Breusch-Pagan test per subject
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Residual variance differs systematically across subjects due to unmodeled factors (e.g., activity, circadian phase, trait variability). A homoscedastic model forces a single variance estimate, miscalibrating uncertainty. After controlling for known variance predictors (activity, time of day), the remaining subject-specific variance should be modeled hierarchically: each subject has its own variance parameter drawn from a population distribution. This yields calibrated subject-specific prediction intervals and improves uncertainty quantification.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Hierarchical Bayesian models or mixed-effects location-scale models are appropriate. Minimum 30 observations per subject for reliable variance estimation. Check for non-Gaussian residuals; consider Student-t errors. Variance predictors should be included in the scale model.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Sensor firmware version differences introduce systematic bias across devices used by different subjects.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Firmware updates change filtering, sampling rate, or calibration constants; subjects receiving devices with different firmware experience shifted feature distributions, degrading model performance for those cohorts.
control_variables: Firmware version string per device per subject per session
Device age (days since manufacture or first use)
Battery level at start of session
rival_explanations: Subject physiological differences coincidentally aligned with firmware cohorts
Environmental differences between cohorts (e.g., different study sites)
Software preprocessing pipeline changes concurrent with firmware update
minimum_data_needed: Firmware version logged for every recording session
Feature distributions (HRV, EDA metrics) stratified by firmware version
Model performance metrics (AUC, calibration) per firmware version
Sufficient subjects per firmware version (>=20) for statistical comparison
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Firmware updates alter digital filtering (e.g., PPG bandpass), sampling rate, or calibration coefficients, shifting the feature distribution. After controlling for hardware revision, device age, battery, and temperature, the firmware version acts as a domain shift. The model should include firmware version as a categorical covariate, apply domain adaptation (e.g., CORAL, adversarial), or recalibrate features per firmware using a small labeled subset. Firmware should be standardized across study or treated as a blocking factor.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Firmware logs must be automated (device reports version on each sync). Hardware revision is critical because same firmware on different hardware may behave differently. Battery voltage affects LED intensity in PPG. Temperature affects analog components. Preprocessing pipeline version must be tracked alongside firmware.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Physical activity intensity interacts with stress detection, and habitual activity patterns differ per subject.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: High-intensity movement generates artifacts that overlap with stress signatures; subjects with more vigorous daily routines produce noisier stress windows, increasing uncertainty.
possible_confounders: Activity type (cycling, weightlifting, walking) - different artifact profiles
Fitness level (fit individuals have lower HR at same workload)
Body composition (adipose tissue affects PPG signal quality)
Sensor placement tightness (looser during vigorous activity)
control_variables: Accelerometer-derived activity intensity (METs, ENMO, or activity counts)
Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max estimate or submaximal test)
Habitual activity level (IPAQ or accelerometer average)
Body mass index and wrist circumference
rival_explanations: Motion artifacts due to loose fit rather than activity intensity per se
Stress-induced movement (fidgeting, pacing) confounded with activity
Model not trained on high-activity stress examples
minimum_data_needed: Synchronized high-resolution accelerometer (>=25 Hz) and physiological data
Activity type labels (from annotation or validated classifier)
Fitness assessment per subject
Per-subject habitual activity pattern (7+ days accelerometer)
Stress labels during varying activity intensities
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Physical activity generates motion artifacts and physiological changes (increased HR, decreased HRV, increased SCL) that overlap with stress signatures. The artifact magnitude and physiological response depend on activity intensity (METs), type (rhythmic vs. non-rhythmic), and subject fitness. After controlling for activity intensity and type via accelerometer features, fitness, and habitual activity, the residual interaction predicts subject-specific detection uncertainty. The model should include activity intensity as a time-varying covariate, use activity-specific artifact rejection, and potentially train separate classifiers for high-activity vs. low-activity contexts.
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Activity intensity must be measured concurrently (accelerometer). Fitness level modulates HR response at given workload. Habitual activity determines exposure to high-artifact conditions. Activity type matters: weightlifting causes large non-rhythmic artifacts; cycling causes rhythmic artifacts. Sensor tightness often decreases during vigorous activity.

enriched_hypotheses.original_hypothesis: Data missingness not at random (e.g., device removal during high stress) varies by subject, biasing uncertainty estimates.
enriched_hypotheses.original_mechanism: Subjects who find the device uncomfortable during stressful episodes remove it, causing systematic loss of high-stress windows; the model then sees a truncated stress distribution, inflating uncertainty for those subjects.
possible_confounders: Device comfort and ergonomics (strap material, weight, size)
Occupational constraints (e.g., cannot wear in sterile environment)
control_variables: Wear time per day (hours) from device logs
rival_explanations: Missingness due to technical failure (Bluetooth disconnect, memory full)
Random non-compliance unrelated to stress
Data sync failures (phone not nearby)
minimum_data_needed: Per-subject per-day wear time (from device onboard logging)
Reasons for removal (ecological momentary assessment at removal or retrospective)
Stress labels for periods when device was worn vs. missing (if any proxy)
Device diagnostic logs (battery, Bluetooth, memory)
Comfort and irritation ratings over time
enriched_hypotheses.enriched_mechanism: Missingness is informative (MNAR) when removal probability depends on unobserved stress level. Subjects with low comfort tolerance remove device during high-stress episodes, truncating the upper tail of their stress distribution. After controlling for comfort, irritation, battery, occupation, and forgetfulness, the residual missingness-stress association predicts bias in uncertainty estimates. The analysis should use selection models (e.g., Heckman) or inverse probability weighting with a missingness model predicted by observed covariates and, if available, proxy stress during missing periods (e.g., from phone usage, location).
enriched_hypotheses.enrichment_notes: Wear time must be logged on device (not just phone) to capture off-phone periods. Reasons for removal should be captured in real-time (e.g., button press + prompt) to avoid recall bias. Battery life is a major driver of systematic missingness (overnight charging). Occupation constraints create predictable missingness patterns.
